topic: Following the tie-break proposal: publishing the solver, the

messages.content:
Following up on the corpus post. I went back at the Stage 2 solver and it now settles all 200 of the sample set; my first attempt settled 55.

What might interest this stream more than the count: the proofs close over no axioms at all. #print axioms returns the empty list, not [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound] — they are chains of congrArg and Eq.symm over the hypothesis, so nothing classical is reachable. The counterexample certificates do use the permitted three, being decide on a finite carrier.

One file, 108,748 bytes, standard library only. No database, no embedded lookup table, no problem-specific case, no LLM call at runtime. Earlier versions of mine carried the ETP implication graph as a bitmap and leaned on the competition's reference solver; both are gone and the result is higher without them.

Caveat worth stating: the 200 is the local sample, not a graded set. About a quarter of the sample are order-5 laws, outside the 4694, so no oracle applies and the solver derives what it needs there.

Method: finite model search for the false ones (carriers 2 to 6 here), critical-pair completion for most of the true ones, ordered superposition with a KBO for the rest. Every derived equation carries the hypothesis applications that prove it, and nothing is emitted unless the path replays and each step's rule is applicable where it claims.

Written by AI agents under my direction: two models, same brief, no contact between them. Both closed the two hardest problems independently, which is the main reason I believe those two. Every figure above was measured by my own tooling, not reported by the models.

Everything is Apache-2.0 and public:

  • solver, prover modules, per-problem results and every measurement: https://github.com/carlok/parsimagma
  • the single file that was submitted: https://github.com/carlok/parsimagma/blob/main/dist/solo/selfcontained/solver.py
  • the code, archived and citable: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22237100
  • the write-up: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22214743

On the earlier thread, since the order of events matters: I argued for ranking on publication when my solver settled 55 of 200, which is to say when the rule could not have helped me. The 200 came a day later. I would rather state that than have it inferred.

Source went up hours after the deadline rather than at it, because two other entrants asked for that and it cost me nothing. Their reasons were theirs to give and I am not restating them here.

messages.content:
the proofs close over no axioms at all.

This is indeed known to always be possible! Godel's completeness theorem says that (among other things), if an implication is true (for possible-infinite magmas), it can always be found by just "equational reasoning" -- repeated substitution and chaining of equations together -- which does not require axioms.

In fact the finite counterexamples also have the property that (in Lean's type theory, in the normal statement as an existential) we can also always give the construction without axioms if we so wish. ... your magmas are almost doing this already, but so much of Lean's automation incidentally brings in axioms, it's easy to miss; it would be pretty easy to adapt any finite magma to be an axiom-free proof. (I bet any frontier LLM could do this for you if you asked it.)

The more interesting case is infinite countermodels. This problem is not known to be decidable in general. (I don't think that the specific question of "does this single equation imply this single equation" is known to be undecidable though either, so there's hope!) A good math research question would be: if x -/-> y for infinite magmas, and we have a proof with the three standard axioms, does that imply a proof without the three standard axioms?

messages.content:
@Alex Meiburg Interesting, I checked one of the infinite countermodels already generated by my Stage 2 solver.
It uses Sum Nat Nat as the carrier, with the source law proved by recursion/case analysis and an explicit witness for failure of the target.

#print axioms submission gives:

submission does not depend on any axioms

So at least for that infinite family, the countermodel certificate is already completely axiom-free. Of course this is only an example, not an answer to the general question you raise.

messages.content:
I checked this against my Stage 2 solver after your comment.
It already contains two infinite-countermodel constructions whose generated Lean certificates are axiom-free.

One is an inductive Sum Nat Nat construction for the 1659 family; the other is a reflection-style infinite construction for the 1167 family. The latter produced axiom-free certificates for two distinct targets in my local corpus.

#print axioms submission returns the empty list in those cases.

Most of my other infinite constructions do pull in propext or the usual three through Mathlib, so this is not just an artifact of the audit. Of course this does not answer the general question you raised, but it gives a couple of concrete constructive examples.
messages.subject: Following the tie-break proposal: publishing the solver, the

messages.content:
I checked this more systematically . I now have five distinct infinite-countermodel constructions with fully axiom-free Lean certificates (#print axioms submission = []): inductive Sum Nat Nat, reflection/involution, central-pair, rectangular-band, and free-semigroup models.

Several more look straightforward to reconstruct the same way once Mathlib automation is removed. So the interesting difficulty may really be the general elimination theorem, not producing concrete axiom-free infinite examples.

The formal proof on the right could use the negation of an equation, among other non equational formulas. But we want an equational proof, using only equations and the usual rules of deduction. This completeness result is due to Birkhoff. We need to define what we mean by equations.

Proof

Let L={⋄}L=\{\diamond\}L={⋄}. A term is just any syntactically valid expression built from variables and ⋄\diamond⋄, so for example x⋄(x⋄x)x\diamond(x\diamond x)x⋄(x⋄x) is a term, while x⋄x⋄xx\diamond x\diamond xx⋄x⋄x is not. Equations have the form ∀x∀y,p(x)=q(y)\forall {x} \forall {y}, p({x}) =q({y})∀x∀y,p(x)=q(y) where x,yx,yx,y are tuples of variables of any size. The quantifiers are usually implicit. Let TTT be a set of equations in language LLL.

Take the free magma F(X)F(X)F(X) on the variables under s,ts,ts,t. Its elements are the formal magma terms themselves, with operation

u⋄F(X)v=(u⋄v).u\diamond^{F(X)}v=(u\diamond v).u⋄F(X)v=(u⋄v).

For every equation p=qp=qp=q in TTT and every substitution σ\sigmaσ of terms for variables, consider the pair

(σ(p),σ(q)).(\sigma(p),\sigma(q)).(σ(p),σ(q)).

Let ≡T\equiv_T≡T​ be the smallest congruence on F(X)F(X)F(X) containing all these pairs. A congruence is an equivalence relation compatible with the magma operation:

u≡Tu′,v≡Tv′⟹u⋄v≡Tu′⋄v′.u\equiv_T u',\quad v\equiv_T v'\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\diamond v\equiv_T u'\diamond v'.u≡T​u′,v≡T​v′⟹u⋄v≡T​u′⋄v′.

There is a smallest such congruence because the intersection of any collection of congruences is again a congruence.

Now form the quotient magma

A=F(X)/≡T.A=F(X)/{\equiv_T}.A=F(X)/≡T​.

Its operation is

[u]⋄[v]=[u⋄v],[u]\diamond[v]=[u\diamond v],[u]⋄[v]=[u⋄v],

which is well defined precisely because ≡T\equiv_T≡T​ is a congruence.
Claim. A⊨TA\models TA⊨T.

Take an equation p=qp=qp=q in TTT and any assignment of its variables in AAA. Every element of AAA has the form [u][u][u] for some term uuu, so choose representatives and write the assignment as

x↦[ux].x\mapsto [u_x].x↦[ux​].

pA=[σ(p)]p^A=[\sigma(p)]pA=[σ(p)]

$$T\models s=t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\vdash_{\mathrm{FOL}}s=t.$$

The formal proof on the right could the negation of an equation, among other non equational formulas. But we want an equational proof, using only equations and the usual rules of deduction. This completeness result is due to Birkhoff. We need to define what we mean by equations.

```spoiler Proof
Let $$L=\{\diamond\}$$. A term is just any syntactically valid expression built from variables and $$\diamond$$, so for example $$x\diamond(x\diamond x)$$ is a term, while $$x\diamond x\diamond x$$ is not. Equations have the form  $$\forall {x} \forall {y},  p({x}) =q({y})$$ where $$x,y$$ are tuples of variables of any size. The quantifiers are usually implicit.  Let $$T$$ be a set of equations in language $$L$$.

Take the free magma $$F(X)$$ on the variables under $$s,t$$. Its elements are the formal magma terms themselves, with operation

$$u\diamond^{F(X)}v=(u\diamond v).$$

For every equation $$p=q$$ in $$T$$ and every substitution $$\sigma$$ of terms for variables, consider the pair

$$(\sigma(p),\sigma(q)).$$

Let $$\equiv_T$$ be the smallest congruence on $$F(X)$$ containing all these pairs. A congruence is an equivalence relation compatible with the magma operation:

$$u\equiv_T u',\quad v\equiv_T v'\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u\diamond v\equiv_T u'\diamond v'.$$

There is a smallest such congruence because the intersection of any collection of congruences is again a congruence.

Now form the quotient magma

$$A=F(X)/{\equiv_T}.$$

Its operation is

$$[u]\diamond[v]=[u\diamond v],$$

which is well defined precisely because $$\equiv_T$$ is a congruence.
**Claim.** $$A\models T$$.

Take an equation $$p=q$$ in $$T$$ and any assignment of its variables in $$A$$. Every element of $$A$$ has the form $$[u]$$ for some term $$u$$, so choose representatives and write the assignment as

$$x\mapsto [u_x].$$

Let $$\sigma$$ be the substitution $$x\mapsto u_x$$. By induction on the construction of terms,

$$p^A=[\sigma(p)]$$

and

$$q^A=[\sigma(q)].$$

But $$\equiv_T$$ contains every substitution instance of every equation in $$T$$, so

$$\sigma(p)\equiv_T\sigma(q).$$

Hence

$$[\sigma(p)]=[\sigma(q)],$$

and therefore $$p^A=q^A$$. Thus $$A\models T$$.



Since $$A\models T$$, the equation $$s=t$$ must hold in $$A$$ under the assignment $$v(x)=x$$ that just sends each variable to its corresponding generator. Hence

$$[s]=[t],$$

so

$$s\equiv_T t.$$

It remains to explain why this means that there is an equational proof.

Let

$$D=\{(u,v):T\vdash_{\mathrm{Eq}}u=v\}.$$

The rules of equational logic make $$D$$ a congruence: reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity make it an equivalence relation, and replacement gives compatibility with $$\diamond$$. Also, by substitution, $$D$$ contains every pair

$$(\sigma(p),\sigma(q))$$

coming from an equation $$p=q$$ in $$T$$.

Therefore $$D$$ is one of the congruences containing all the pairs used to generate $$\equiv_T$$. Since $$\equiv_T$$ is the smallest such congruence,

$$\equiv_T\subseteq D.$$

We already know $$s\equiv_T t$$, so $$(s,t)\in D$$. In other words,

$$T\vdash_{\mathrm{Eq}}s=t.$$

Hence, for any equational theory $$T$$,

$$T\models s=t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\vdash_{\mathrm{Eq}}s=t.$$
```

That was my rough proof sketch for https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birkhoff%27s_theorem_(equational_logic).
